clue.text: Boutique hotel in Provence?

indicators.note: 'In' drops the letter just named inside the word that follows it, so one piece ends up housed within the other.

parts.note: the big city of the French Riviera sits at the eastern edge of Provence, and the question mark owns up to the looseness
H is hotel in the radio alphabet that pilots and police use, alpha bravo charlie delta

explanation.surface: A small stylish hotel somewhere in the south of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' is a letter here rather than a building, and 'Boutique' is being used as an adjective — the sense in 'boutique brewery', not a shop with a window.
explanation.definitionFit: Boutique and niche are both adjectives for a small specialised corner of a market, as in a boutique hotel or a niche product.

clue.text: Undersign leaders of climate legislation in environment terminology

indicators.note: One word doing two jobs: the 'sign' is a piece to be found, and 'under' puts what follows below it, which in a down entry means later in the answer.
The leader of a word is the letter at its front, so two words named here surrender one letter each.

parts.note: the natural world is nature, and environment is the everyday word for the same thing
an omen is a sign of what is coming, the portent sense of the word

indicators.note: 'In' asks for the pieces already found to be dropped inside the word that comes after it.

parts.note: the front letter of each of these two words, taken in the order given

explanation.surface: Signing off on the first green bills, in the language environmental policy uses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undersign' looks like one word about signatures and is really two instructions run together, and 'environment' is the natural world rather than the political one the surface is talking about.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomenclature is the system of names a field uses for the things in it, which is what terminology means in any specialist subject.

clue.text: Disease can be horrific if ignored by family member

indicators.note: 'Can be' says the material is capable of coming out as something else, which is a licence to move its letters around.
What is ignored is passed over and never used, so the two letters spelling that little word leave the material.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material with two struck out, and the six left over reshuffled
sis is the familiar short form of sister
the I and the F come out of the material before any shuffling starts

explanation.surface: A warning that an illness turns nasty when relatives take no notice of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horrific' reads as a comment on the disease and is the material itself, while the word sitting inside it is the one the clue tells you to throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: Cirrhosis is the scarring of the liver that follows long damage, usually from alcohol, so 'disease' names it by its plainest category.

clue.text: Wax lyrical about the previous bunch getting a comeback

indicators.note: Something making a comeback arrives back the way it went, so the letters just found are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: an ex is the previous partner, and ex- is the prefix for anything former
a bunch of something is a lot of it, here written back to front

explanation.surface: Praising a former band whose old records are selling again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like an instruction to wrap one piece around another, and it is only the 'concerning' of waxing lyrical about a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: To extol is to praise something warmly and at length, which is exactly what waxing lyrical about it means.

clue.text: Our secret repository tapes got interfered with

indicators.note: Something interfered with has been meddled about until it is no longer as it was left, and letters left in that state do not keep their order.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material, the two words run together

explanation.surface: A hiding place for our secrets, whose tapes somebody has tampered with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Between you, me and the gatepost' is the British phrase for saying something in confidence, which is what makes a gatepost the keeper of a secret.
explanation.definitionFit: Say a thing is between you, me and the gatepost and the gatepost is where the secret is lodged, so it stands as our confidential store.

clue.text: Conk out drunk, get up and use loo? Not us!

indicators.note: Read 'us' as the plural of the letter U: both of them are struck out of the material before the rest is rearranged.
A drunk cannot hold a straight line, and letters in that condition will not keep to the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: five letters with the U struck out, leaving four to work with
six letters with the second U struck out, leaving five

explanation.surface: We are not the sort to pass out drunk and then stagger up to the loo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Us' is not the pronoun it looks like — it is the plural of the letter U, and the eye reads straight past that while the clue quietly removes two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To conk out is to stop dead or drop off, and of a person it means dropping into sleep, usually all at once.

definitions.note: A span of numerals stands in for a word: the setter is pointing at the shared ending of those numbers' names rather than offering a synonym.

indicators.note: The division sign is read as English rather than arithmetic: it cuts the numeral in two, and the letter named after it goes into the cut.

parts.note: X is ten in Roman numerals
the letter is taken at face value out of the equation

explanation.surface: A scrap of algebra, X over e, coming out somewhere in a range of numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: Roman numerals are ordinary crossword words — X for ten, C for a hundred — and the mathematical symbols here are read as English, with 'divided by' meaning split open.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirteen to nineteen are the numbers whose names all finish with these four letters, so the range points at the ending they share.

clue.text: You or me on vacation, creative and articulate

parts.note: both of these little words belong to that part of speech, so the clue names the class by handing over two of its members

indicators.note: A house whose people are on vacation has nothing left but its shell, so the word keeps its first and last letters and loses everything between.

parts.note: the letters at the two ends of the word, with the middle cleared out

explanation.surface: You and I away on holiday, inventive and clear-spoken with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You or me on vacation' looks like one phrase about a holiday, and the emptying instruction actually reaches forward past the comma to work on the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce a word is to sound it out distinctly, and 'articulate' as a verb means exactly that, saying a thing clearly.

clue.text: Some fires, in general, burn

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a portion of what follows rather than the whole of it, and the portion wanted is an unbroken run of letters.

parts.note: the run starts on the last letter of the first word, swallows the two-letter word whole and stops two letters into the third

explanation.surface: Fires burning here and there, spoken of in general terms.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas do the camouflage: they break the words into a remark about fires when the three of them are one continuous row of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To singe is to burn something only at its surface, so 'burn' defines it as the plain verb with the depth taken out.

clue.text: At first, Harry Potter got embroiled with emotion of greater relevance

indicators.note: To be embroiled is to be tangled up in something, and letters tangled together come apart in a new order.
'At first' takes only what stands at the front, so the name beside it hands over its opening letter and nothing else.

parts.note: the opening letter of the name, which is all the instruction before it asks for
six letters of raw material, the surname taken whole
seven more letters of raw material, the word as it stands

explanation.surface: Harry Potter dragged into a row that turns emotional.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks as though it governs the whole name, and it takes only the H — the surname goes into the mixture entire, which is where the extra letters come from.
explanation.definitionFit: 'More to the point' is the idiom for what bears harder on the matter under discussion, so it works as a whole phrase rather than word by word.

clue.text: Those with charts choose to hide book? Stirs trouble

indicators.note: To hide a thing is to put it out of sight inside something else, so one piece goes bodily within the word before it.
Trouble is disorder, and letters in disorder do not stay in the arrangement the clue gave them.

parts.note: a tome is a big heavy volume
five letters of raw material, stirred into another order
to opt for something is to choose it

explanation.surface: People with charts choosing to conceal a book, which stirs up bother.
explanation.walkthrough: The charts are the boards of shrinking letters you read out from across the room, not tables of figures, and 'Stirs trouble' reads as one phrase while working as material plus instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Optometrists test eyesight for a living and the letter chart on the wall is the tool of the trade, so they are named by it.

clue.text: Sceptic rogue exposed Philistine

indicators.note: A rogue element has broken ranks and gone its own way, so the letters beside it abandon the order they were in.
Someone exposed has had their covering stripped off, so the word loses the letter standing at each end.

parts.note: the setter's own pen name with its outermost letter taken off each end, leaving eight

explanation.surface: A headline: a rogue doubter has shown somebody up as a boor.
explanation.walkthrough: Philistine is the setter's pseudonym, printed above the puzzle, and the clue makes fodder of it — a Guardian setter signing the grid from inside one of its answers.
explanation.definitionFit: A nihilist rejects every belief and value as groundless, which makes 'sceptic' a fair if understated word for the doubter it names.

clue.text: Smell and look of a shepherd

definitions.note: The definition names a class where the answer is one particular member of it, a nursery-rhyme girl, so the fit is by example rather than by synonym.

parts.note: BO is body odour, the initials British advertising made unmentionable
a peep is a quick furtive look

explanation.surface: The scent and the appearance of somebody who watches over sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Bo Peep is the nursery-rhyme girl who lost her sheep, which is why the strays she mislaid are sitting two rows below her in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Bo Peep of the rhyme keeps sheep and loses them, so she is a shepherd named as one individual rather than described as a type.

clue.text: Strays see plot unravel, keeping quiet

indicators.note: Something unravelling comes apart thread by thread, so what it touches does not stay in the order it was wound in.
What is kept is held on to, so the letters named next stay in the mixture instead of dropping out of it.

parts.note: seven letters of raw material, the two words together
sh is the noise you make when asking for quiet

explanation.surface: Watching a story fall apart and saying nothing at all about it.
explanation.walkthrough: A lost sheep is a person who has wandered off from the fold, the parable's sense, and the shepherd two rows above in this grid is the one who mislaid them.
explanation.definitionFit: Strays are animals that have wandered from where they belong, and lost sheep are exactly that, both words in the plural.

clue.text: Of course their guns misfired

indicators.note: A gun that misfires has not gone off the way it was loaded, so the letters come out other than as they went in.

parts.note: nine letters of raw material, the two words run together

explanation.surface: A resigned account of a skirmish in which every weapon on their side failed.
explanation.walkthrough: Definition and answer are both things people say rather than things they mean, and 'a sure thing' carries a second sense the gambler uses: a certainty.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Sure thing' is the spoken agreement meaning yes, certainly, which is the job 'of course' does in the same conversation.

clue.text: Desperately, I phone agency in old Lebanon

indicators.note: Doing a thing desperately is doing it without order or plan, so the letters land in whatever arrangement comes.

parts.note: six letters of raw material, the pronoun and the verb together
the CIA is the American foreign intelligence service

explanation.surface: A frantic call put through to the intelligence services.
explanation.walkthrough: Phoenicia was the seafaring civilisation of Tyre and Sidon on what is now the Lebanese coast, and its traders gave Europe the alphabet these letters are written in.
explanation.definitionFit: Phoenicia was the ancient name for the coastal strip that is Lebanon today, so 'old Lebanon' names the same ground at an earlier date.

clue.text: Snack shop unwrapped snack

indicators.note: Unwrapping takes the covering off both ends at once, so each word beside it gives up its outermost letters and keeps the middle.

parts.note: one letter off each end of the five, leaving the three in the middle
the same treatment on the second word, its two middle letters left standing

explanation.surface: Something bought at a snack shop and already out of its packet.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word opens and closes the clue doing two different jobs: the first is material to be trimmed, the last is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nacho is a single tortilla chip served with melted cheese or salsa, so 'snack' names it by the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Nations, My Lord, rise in revolution

indicators.note: A revolution overturns the established order, so the word beside it comes back in a different arrangement.

parts.note: a count is the continental nobleman, of the rank a lord is addressed by
four letters of raw material, turned about into another order

explanation.surface: Somebody telling a judge that the nations are rising in revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise in revolution' reads as one phrase about an uprising and is material plus instruction, and 'My Lord' wants the rank rather than the person being addressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Countries and nations are both plurals for sovereign states, though 'nation' leans on the people and 'country' on the territory they hold.

clue.text: Team swears regularly? That's a shocker!

indicators.note: Doing a thing regularly is doing it at a fixed interval, so letters are picked at every other position instead of in a run.

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of the two words read as one string

explanation.surface: A side whose players are forever cursing, which is quite a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's a shocker' reads as tabloid outrage at the language and means a thing that delivers a shock — the setter's electricity, not the newspaper's.
explanation.definitionFit: A taser fires darts that deliver an incapacitating electric shock, so 'a shocker' names it by the one thing it does.

clue.text: Sue's verse lacking charm, then?

parts.note: writing with the verse taken out of it is prose, a definition by opposite rather than by synonym
cute means charming or appealing, the adjective beside the noun

explanation.surface: Sue's poetry, it seems, has no charm about it at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sue' is a woman's name on the surface and a verb underneath, and the first half of the wordplay is defined by what it lacks, which is rarer than a straight synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To sue is to take somebody to law and to prosecute is to bring the case against them, both being the verb for hauling a person into court.

clue.text: Distant memory about author's return

indicators.note: To be about a thing is to be all round it, so the word before this one closes over the letters that follow.
What returns comes back the way it went, so the two letters named here are written in the opposite order.

parts.note: learning by rote is memorising through repetition, so rote does duty for memory
the person writing the clue is ME, and here those two letters run backwards

explanation.surface: A faint recollection of a writer making a comeback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author' is the setter referring to themselves, one of the oldest conventions in the craft — writer, compiler and yours truly all mean the same two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something remote is far off, whether in miles or in likelihood, and 'distant' is the plain adjective for it in either sense.

clue.text: Cruel treatment essentially deliberate

parts.note: a mean act is a cruel one, the unkind sense of the word rather than the average

indicators.note: What is essential sits at the heart of a thing, so the letter at the very centre of the word is the one taken.

parts.note: the middle letter of the nine, with four standing either side of it

explanation.surface: Harsh handling that was entirely intended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliberate' is the adjective here and not the verb you hear first, and 'cruel treatment' reads as a single phrase while working as two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Something meant is something intended rather than accidental, which is what calling an act deliberate says about it.

clue.text: Perhaps grandma to some extent dances to relax

indicators.note: 'To some extent' means part of what is there rather than all of it, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow.

parts.note: eight letters running unbroken from one letter into the first word as far as the opening letter of the last

explanation.surface: A grandmother who does a certain amount of dancing to unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is a fair-play flag rather than padding: a grandmother is one example of the class the answer names, not a synonym for the whole of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is one of the forebears a person is descended from, so the clue defines the general word by handing over a single instance.

clue.text: Precise demand

definitions.meaning: the adjective for something correct down to the last detail
the verb for wringing a payment or a promise out of somebody who would rather not give it

explanation.surface: A demand worded down to the very last detail.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like an adjective describing a noun, and they are two independent senses standing side by side, one adjective and one verb.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the adjective for something correct to the last detail; the other is the verb meaning to wring a payment out of somebody.

clue.text: This erupts frequently in Vietnam

indicators.note: 'In' says the letters wanted are already sitting inside the word that follows, in the order they are written there.

parts.note: four consecutive letters beginning at the third letter of the country's name

explanation.surface: A report of something going off again and again in Vietnam.
explanation.walkthrough: The volcano is Sicilian, so 'in Vietnam' is geography for the surface only and the country's name is a row of letters rather than a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the Sicilian volcano that erupts more often than any other in Europe, so the clue names it by its habit.

clue.text: Poor governments giving Socrates a kick, I fancy

indicators.note: 'Fancy' asks you to imagine the material as something other than what is written, so its order is not to be trusted.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material, the philosopher's name taken whole
five more letters, the article counted in with them
the pronoun contributes itself, the fourteenth letter needed

explanation.surface: Somebody picturing a good boot aimed at Socrates and at incompetent governments.
explanation.walkthrough: A kakistocracy is rule by the worst people, from the Greek kakistos meaning worst, which is why a Greek philosopher is standing in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A kakistocracy is a state run by its worst citizens, so 'poor governments' names them in the plural by the quality of whoever governs.

clue.text: Marks floral parts

definitions.meaning: the wounds said to appear on the hands and feet of certain saints, mirroring the crucifixion
the sticky tips of a flower's pistil, where the pollen has to land

explanation.surface: An examiner awarding grades to the various bits of a flower.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are the plural of stigma, one out of religion and one out of botany, and the clue sets them side by side so the first reads as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the marks of Christ's wounds appearing on a body; the other is the plural of the flower's pollen-catching stigma.

clue.text: Finally grant requests for jobs

indicators.note: 'Finally' points at what comes at the very end, so only the closing letter of the next word is taken.

parts.note: the closing letter of the word, which is all the instruction wants
to request is to ask, and both words stay in the third person

explanation.surface: An official giving way at last and approving applications for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally grant requests' reads as a bureaucrat giving in after a long wait, which is what makes the first word look like an adverb of time rather than a letter-picking instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks are pieces of work set for somebody to do, and 'jobs' is the everyday plural for the same things.
